cues.text: The year before the full -scale invasion, Russia supplied about 3 % of US crude oil imports.
But Russia was one of the world's big oil exporters.
Picture a refinery that ordinarily buys Russian crude.
After the invasion, some buyers backed away from Russian oil.
If that refinery still needs to keep running, it has to find another seller.
Now picture a second refinery that already buys from that seller, it suddenly has more competition for the next cargo.
The second refinery can pay more even though it never bought a Russian barrel.
And that bidding can start before a shipment actually goes missing.
If you're responsible for keeping a refinery running next month, waiting to see what happens is a risk of its own.
Oil prices jumped before the agency had recorded a loss of supply.
Crude oil is the biggest single cost in a gallon of gasoline.
When crude gets more expensive, a station can end up paying more for its next delivery.
gasoline demand had already picked up earlier in the year.
That left less fuel on hand to meet demand, which also helped push up pump prices.
The fuel bill reaches further than the driver's seat.
A truck hauling flour to a bakery runs on fuel too.
When diesel costs more, a carrier may charge more to make that same trip.
By the time you see a loaf on a shelf, somebody has already paid to move the ingredients and to deliver the finished bread.
In Ukraine, an even bigger problem was getting grain out in the first place.
Before the invasion, Russia and Ukraine together accounted for roughly 30 % of the wheat sold abroad.
When Russia blocked Ukraine's Black Sea ports, grain could still be sitting in storage while a buyer overseas scrambled to fill an order.
Some exports moved by rail and through ports on the Danube River.
A mill that has to keep making flour can look for wheat somewhere else.
So can all the other mills facing the same problem?
They can end up bidding against one another for wheat that was already going to be sold.
That's how a port closure can affect the price of grain grown in a completely different country.
In March, international wheat prices jumped nearly 20 % in a month.
Concerns about the American crop were adding pressure at the same time.
On August 1st, a ship called the Razoni left the Ukrainian port of Odesa carrying corn.
It was the first commercial grain shipment under a deal signed in July to let food sail out of three Ukrainian ports again.
The price of wheat on world markets had already fallen in July.
The United Nations Food Agency pointed to the deal and to new harvests becoming available in the Northern Hemisphere.
Buyers could see more grain coming onto the market before that first ship had even left.
That same July, the US Bureau of Labor Statistics recorded an increase in bread prices.
Say a bakery ordered the flour for today's bread weeks ago.
If the price of wheat falls this morning, the bakery still owes what it agreed to pay for the flower.
It has to keep the ovens running either way.
On the bakery's next order, flour might be cheaper, but if it's paying more to get the bread to the store, part of that saving could disappear on the truck.
The retailer has bills of its own.
By the time you pick up the loaf, the price on the shelf reflects decisions made at each step, sometimes weeks apart.
If your shift starts before the first bus, there's only so much you can do about how often you fill up.
You can put less gas in the tank today.
That just means you'll be back at the station sooner.
When a few dollars more for gas comes out of a paycheck that's already spoken for, it can mean putting off something else you need.
Maybe the shoes you were going to replace have to last another month.
In Somalia that year, drought had damaged local harvests.
It also meant neighboring countries had less food to sell.
Somalia relied heavily on imported grain, including wheat from Russia and Ukraine.
The World Food Program and the United Nations Food and Agriculture Agency reported that rising global food and fuel prices piled onto those local problems.
